query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with density below 6 g/cm3, the metastable, supersaturated solid solution evolves during low-to-intermediate temperature exposure (roughly 150–350°C) by partitioning Mg to grain boundaries and precipitating Mg-rich intermetallics together with Cu/Zn-enriched phases. This chemical and structural partitioning simultaneously (i) increases room-temperature corrosion via microgalvanic coupling and intergranular pathways and (ii) decreases high-temperature oxidation rates by lowering the effective Mg activity at the surface, enabling formation of a more continuous Al-rich (alumina/spinel) scale. The structural mediator of this behavior is nanoscale precipitation and boundary segregation that alters both near-surface composition and local electrochemical heterogeneity.
generation.material_initial_state: As-quenched, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g., Al–Mg–(Cu/Zn)–(Ti/Sn/Gd) family) with supersaturated solid solution, minimal long-range ordered intermetallics, fine solute clusters, and homogeneous near-surface composition; density < 6 g/cm3.
generation.intervention: Controlled isothermal aging (e.g., 200–300°C for 10–24 h) to drive partitioning and precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallics and Cu/Zn-enriched phases, plus grain-boundary segregation; no change in bulk composition.
generation.conditions: Two-sample controlled comparison: (A) as-quenched metastable state; (B) aged state under identical composition and density. Evaluate (i) corrosion in aerated 3.5 wt% NaCl at room temperature; (ii) oxidation at 600–700°C in dry air for fixed durations (e.g., 10–50 h).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallics and Cu/Zn-enriched phases, plus Mg segregation to grain boundaries and near-surface regions, which reduces Mg in the matrix near the free surface and increases chemical heterogeneity at the microscale.
generation.mechanism: Aging-induced partitioning decreases the chemical activity of Mg at the surface, favoring selective oxidation of Al and formation of more continuous Al-rich oxides (alumina and/or Mg–Al spinel), thereby reducing oxidation kinetics. Concurrently, the emergence of Mg-rich and Cu/Zn-rich second phases at grain boundaries and within grains increases local galvanic potential differences and provides fast paths for electrolyte ingress, raising the corrosion rate and promoting intergranular attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-quenched baseline: after aging, (1) corrosion rate increases (directional increase; magnitude uncertain), with more localized/intergranular features; passive film becomes less stable in chloride. (2) High-temperature oxidation rate decreases (directional decrease; magnitude uncertain), and the oxide scale becomes more Al-rich and continuous with less MgO dominance. Near-surface composition shows reduced Mg activity in the matrix and increased partitioning into discrete phases.
generation.baseline: As-quenched metastable solid solution exhibits comparatively lower corrosion due to microstructural homogeneity but higher oxidation rates due to Mg-rich, less-protective oxides forming under high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Effects are expected when Al content is sufficient to form protective Al-rich oxides (e.g., > ~25 at% Al) and Mg content is high enough to drive precipitation/segregation upon aging (e.g., > ~10 at% Mg). The predicted oxidation improvement applies to 500–800°C in dry air; in very Mg-lean alloys or those dominated by elements that form highly protective oxides (e.g., very high Ti), or at temperatures where Zn volatility or phase melting dominates, the trends may weaken or reverse. Rapid surface depletion/enrichment due to processing (e.g., machining, severe deformation) could also alter outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of changes (percent increase/decrease) depends on exact composition, precipitate identity/volume fraction, grain size, and aging schedule; specific intermetallic species and oxide phase fractions are composition-sensitive. Without composition-resolved prior data here, only directional predictions are supported.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a single HEA composition (density < 6 g/cm3) in the as-quenched metastable state. Split into two groups: (A) retain as-quenched; (B) age at 250°C for 16 h. Characterize microstructure (TEM, STEM-EDS, APT) and near-surface composition (XPS/SIMS). Test corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl at RT (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS; assess intergranular attack by SEM) and oxidation at 650°C in dry air (thermogravimetry, post-oxidation XRD/Raman and cross-sectional SEM/EDS to identify oxide phases and continuity).
measurements: TEM/STEM-EDS/APT: detect Mg-rich and Cu/Zn-enriched precipitates and grain-boundary segregation after aging versus as-quenched
XPS/SIMS of near-surface: quantify relative Mg vs Al activities before/after aging
Potentiodynamic polarization: corrosion current density and breakdown potential in 3.5 wt% NaCl at RT
EIS: passive film resistance/capacitance and defect density
SEM after corrosion: evidence of intergranular attack/localized pitting density
TGA: oxidation mass gain at 650°C over time
XRD/Raman and cross-sectional SEM/EDS: oxide phase identification (Al2O3/MgAl2O4 versus MgO) and scale continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following hold under the stated conditions: (i) Aging does not produce measurable Mg partitioning (no increase in Mg-rich precipitates or boundary segregation) compared to as-quenched; (ii) Corrosion current density of the aged sample is equal to or lower than the as-quenched sample, and breakdown potential shifts nobler, indicating improved corrosion resistance; (iii) Oxidation mass gain for the aged sample is equal to or higher than the as-quenched sample at 650°C, and the oxide remains MgO-dominated or shows no increase in Al-rich oxide continuity relative to the baseline.
